In [44]:
 #set things up to save frames to a movie:
    
    # fig = the figure the writer will record from
    # 'swarm.mp4' = the name of the movie file to save
    # 100 = dpi (dots per inch)

with writer.saving(fig, 'swarm.mp4', 100):
    
    # Create an array for centroids
    center_arr = np.linspace(-7, 7, 26)
    # loop 25 times
    for i, center in enumerate(center_arr): #sets i as the index number and center as the element in center_arr 
        
        # clear the previous plot
        plt.cla()
        
        # create the x array
        x= np.random.normal(center, size=[1,1000])
        
        # create the y array
        y= -1*np.random.normal(center, size=[1,1000])
        
        #print(f" at i = {i}, x = {x} and y = {y}")
        #checking the points
        
        # plot the x and y values
        plt.scatter(x, y, color="black")
        plt.axis('scaled')
        plt.xlim(-7,7)
        plt.ylim(-7,7)
        # Provide an update of how far we've gone
        if i % 5 == 0:
            print(f'writing frame #{i}: centered at {center:.1f},{center:.1f}')
            #getting a progress update when the code is running
        
        # save the current plot as one frame of the movie
        writer.grab_frame()

    filename = f'flipbook/image{i:02}.jpg'

for i in range(N):
    # plot the current point
    plt.scatter(t[i], y[i], color='black', s=100)
    # plot the line up to this point
    plt.plot(t[0:i+1], y[0:i+1], color='orange', linewidth=2, alpha=0.5)
    plt.xlabel("$t$")
    plt.ylabel("$\sin(t)$")
    plt.title(f'This is frame #{i:02}')
    
    # set the x- & y-limits explicitly, so Python doesn't change them
    plt.ylim(-1.1, 1.1)
    plt.xlim(np.min(t)-1, np.max(t)+1)
    
    # save to a filename that depends on the frame number
    filename = f'flipbook/image{i:02}.jpg'
    print(f'Saving a plot to {filename}')
    plt.savefig(filename, dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")  
    # clear the axes (= the plot rectangle)
    plt.cla()

import matplotlib.animation as ani

FFMpegWriter = ani.writers['ffmpeg'] # pull out the definition of a movie-maker CLASS

writer = FFMpegWriter(fps=10) # create a movie write OBJECT, set frames per second

myImage = plt.figure() # create a blank figure object (e.g. blank piece of paper)

myImage.patch.set_alpha(1.0) # this is just a Python bug fix... don't worry about it

with writer.saving(myImage, "sine.mp4", 150):
    
    for i in range(len(t)):

        # Same plotting code as before
        plt.plot(t[0:i+1], y[0:i+1], color='orange', linewidth=2, alpha=0.5)
        plt.scatter(t[i], y[i], color='black', s=100)
        plt.title(f'This is frame #{i:02}')
        plt.ylim(-1.1,1.1)
        plt.xlim(np.min(t)-1, np.max(t)+1)
        
        writer.grab_frame() # add the plot to the movie

        #plt.cla() # clear the axes

myImage2 = plt.figure() # create a blank figure object (e.g. blank piece of paper)

myImage2.patch.set_alpha(1.0) # this is just a Python bug fix... don't worry about it

with writer.saving(myImage2, 'swarm.mp4', 100):
    
    # Create an array for centroids
    center_arr = np.linspace(-7, 7, 26)
    # loop 25 times
    for i, center in enumerate(center_arr): #sets i as the index number and center as the element in center_arr 
        
        # clear the previous plot
        plt.cla()
        
        # create the x array
        x= np.random.normal(center, size=[1,1000])
        
        # create the y array
        y= -1*np.random.normal(center, size=[1,1000])
        
        #print(f" at i = {i}, x = {x} and y = {y}")
        #checking the points
        
        # plot the x and y values
        plt.scatter(x, y, color="black")
        plt.axis('scaled')
        plt.xlim(-7,7)
        plt.ylim(-7,7)
        # Provide an update of how far we've gone
        if i % 5 == 0:
            print(f'writing frame #{i}: centered at {center:.1f},{center:.1f}')
            #getting a progress update when the code is running
        
        # save the current plot as one frame of the movie
        writer.grab_frame()

# Set directory to the kepler directory where you unzipped the files
# or leave as is if kepler/ is in the same directory as this tutorial
# (Be sure to use \\ for directories if on Windows.)
directory = 'kepler/'
#this took forever for me to figure out but I finally did it after re reading the pseudo code like 8 times
filename = "test.npy"
# load this file into time and flux arrays
time, flux = np.load(directory + filename)
# clear the existing axes (even if they don't exist yet!)
plt.cla()
# make the plot, add labels, set the limits
plt.plot(time, flux)
plt.title(filename)
plt.xlabel('Time (BJD)')
plt.ylabel('Relative Brightness of Star')
plt.ylim(0.99, 1.01)
# adjust the spacing around the plot, to make it look prettier
plt.tight_layout()
# save the current figure out to a single file
output_filename = 'lightcurve-plots/plot-test.png'
plt.savefig(output_filename)
# in addition to writing the plot to a file, show it in your notebook
plt.show()

import matplotlib.animation as ani

FFMpegWriter = ani.writers['ffmpeg'] # pull out the definition of a movie-maker CLASS

writer = FFMpegWriter(fps=1) # create a movie write OBJECT, set to 1 frame per second so I can actually analyze the light curves

myImage = plt.figure() # create a blank figure object (e.g. blank piece of paper)

myImage.patch.set_alpha(1.0) # this is just a Python bug fix... don't worry about it

with writer.saving(myImage, "light_curve.mp4", 150):
    
       
    for i in range(9):
        
        directory = 'kepler/'
        #this took forever for me to figure out but I finally did it after re reading the pseudo code like 8 times
        filename = filenames[i]
        # load this file into time and flux arrays
        time, flux = np.load(filename)
        # clear the existing axes (even if they don't exist yet!)
        plt.cla()
        # make the plot, add labels, set the limits
        plt.plot(time, flux)
        plt.title(f"lightcurve-plots/plot-0{i}.png,")
        plt.xlabel('Time (BJD)')
        plt.ylabel('Relative Brightness of Star')
        plt.ylim(0.99, 1.01)
        # adjust the spacing around the plot, to make it look prettier
        plt.tight_layout()
        # save the current figure out to a single file
        output_filename = 'lightcurve-plots/plot-test.png'
        plt.savefig(output_filename)
        # in addition to writing the plot to a file, show it in your notebook
        writer.grab_frame()

        plt.xlabel('Time (BJD)')
        plt.ylabel('Relative Brightness of Star')
        plt.ylim(0.99, 1.01)
        # adjust the spacing around the plot, to make it look prettier
        plt.tight_layout()
        # save the current figure out to a single file
        output_filename = 'lightcurve-plots/plot-test.png'
        plt.savefig(output_filename)
        # in addition to writing the plot to a file, show it in your notebook
        writer.grab_frame()

for light curve plot 27, I searched on Google, "does KIC1295597 have exoplanet", and found that the system, KIC1295597, does not have any "confirmed exoplanets". This means I was probably just overanalyzing a systematic abnormality.

For light curve plot 34, I searched on Google, "does KIC10329669 have exoplanet", and found that the system, KIC10329669, also does not currently have any exoplanets.

In both cases, I misunderstood what the light curve was representing with "unusual solo bumps". Sadly, I was not able to find the star system with an exoplanet. Also, please know that I significantly slowed down the video by both lowering the frames per second(fps) and playing the video at 0.25x speed. These were the two star systems I identified as having unusual fluctuations in their relative brightness.
